name: Under-eye concealer

lead: Under-eye concealer is a pigmented makeup applied beneath the eyes to cover dark circles, redness and discolouration. Men on forums discuss it as a quick way to look more rested, with an evened tone visible immediately.

It works by covering rather than treating: pigment in the product blends with skin tone to hide discolouration. Concealer is thicker and more pigmented than foundation and meant for small areas. No trial has studied it for dark circles.

paras: Users pick a shade that matches the skin and pat a thin layer under the eyes with a finger, sponge or brush, then blend the edges. Forum posts describe applying it lightly so it does not read as makeup.
No harms are documented in the sources reviewed. Forum posters mention cakey or visible results when the shade or amount is off.

angle.text: Concealer covers dark circles and redness under the eyes with pigment, and the evened tone shows up immediately for a more rested look. It is camouflage that lasts for the day and has no treatment effect.

lead: Under-eye concealer is a pigmented cosmetic applied to the skin beneath the eyes to mask dark circles, redness or discolouration. It is similar to foundation but more heavily pigmented, and is intended for small areas [1][2].

It helps someone look better directly and immediately: by covering or colour-cancelling darkness under the eyes, it can make the face look more rested, brighter and more even, and it requires no procedure, prescription or recovery time. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as an accessible first cosmetic step, with guides on shade matching and on keeping the result from looking like visible makeup, alongside threads about how men can buy and use it discreetly.

Dermatology sources describe dark circles as having several causes, including pigmentation, visible blood vessels, and the structure of the thin lower-eyelid skin and the bone and fat beneath it [3]. A 2021 study of 100 patients examined which factors correlate with the severity of periocular dark circles and with how dissatisfied patients feel about them [4]. Published work on corrective cosmetics exists for other situations, such as skin disease and chemotherapy, but no clinical trial of concealer specifically for under-eye circles was found [5][6].
infobox: Yellow or peach tones for dark circles; green or blue for redness; purple for sallow skin [2]
Max Factor Erace, 1954, per Wikipedia; Covermark, 1930, per Grokipedia [1][2][8]
No trials of concealer for dark circles found

paras: Wikipedia defines concealer as a cosmetic used to mask skin imperfections such as dark circles, blemishes and hyperpigmentation, more heavily pigmented than foundation, which evens out overall skin tone; the two are often used together [2]. Concealers are sold in several formulations aimed at blemishes, scars, redness and under-eye circles [1][2].

Wikipedia lists five common types: liquids in tubes or vials (the most popular, often set with powder to limit creasing), thicker sticks for small areas, creams in pots or palettes applied with a brush, pencils for precise spots, and pressed cream-to-powder compacts applied with a sponge for a matte finish [2]. Heavier-pigmented camouflage makeup is a related category used for birthmarks, scars and vitiligo [2]. Typical ingredients include oils, dimethicone, glycerin, talc, kaolin and water [2].

Some shades match skin tone, while others cancel a specific colour: yellow undertones are used for dark circles, green and blue tints counteract redness from pimples, broken veins or rosacea, and purple-tinted shades can brighten sallow complexions [2]. Common application advice in cosmetic references is to dab a small amount on the area and blend outward with a brush, sponge or fingertips, choosing a shade one or two steps lighter than the skin and setting it with powder [2].

On looksmax.org, shade matching is the recurring theme. A guide thread covers using concealer on dark circles without looking like you are wearing makeup, and another poster describes applying concealer the day before and sleeping in it, then finding it looked cakey up close when a relative noticed. In the 2021 patient study, concealer use was one of the factors linked to higher subjective dissatisfaction with dark circles, alongside female sex, higher Fitzpatrick skin type and fewer hours of sleep; the study reports correlations, not an effect of concealer [4].

Grokipedia traces camouflage cosmetics to ancient Egypt and Greece and credits Lydia O'Leary with Covermark in 1930, originally marketed for scars and birthmarks; Grokipedia is AI-generated and its claims are unverified [1]. Wikipedia's biography of O'Leary describes her as an American entrepreneur born in 1900 in Bedford, Massachusetts, with a large port-wine stain on her face, who received a US patent for her covering foundation in 1932 after an initial rejection on appeal; she later worked with plastic surgeons and dermatologists on wartime rehabilitation, and in the 1980s Covermark marketed to men and children as well as women [7].

Wikipedia gives Max Factor's Erace, launched in 1954, as the first commercially available concealer, citing a 2012 book on the company [2]. Wikipedia's article on Max Factor places Erace in a line of the company's film-derived products that began with a flexible greasepaint developed in 1914 for motion pictures, Pan-Cake in 1937-38 for Technicolor, and Pan-Stik in 1948; the company was founded in 1909 by Maksymilian Faktorowicz [8]. The accounts differ in what they count as a concealer.

Wikipedia's article on periorbital dark circles lists a range of contributors: the bony structure and thin lower-eyelid skin, allergies and eye rubbing, excess melanin and sun exposure, medications that dilate blood vessels, fatigue and sleep loss, and ageing changes including loss of collagen and fat [3]. It also mentions iron and vitamin B12 shortfalls as believed contributors, with weak sourcing for that section [3]. Pigmented, vascular and structural types are commonly distinguished.

Medical treatments described in the same article include eye creams with caffeine or vitamin C, laser and intense pulsed light, low-level laser, fat transplantation and hyaluronic acid fillers; it also notes that hydroquinone, once used in lightening creams, was banned for that purpose in European countries and had its over-the-counter approval revoked by the US FDA in 2006 [3]. Concealer differs from these in that it works only while on the skin and does not alter the underlying cause [3].

A 1988 paper in Cutis by a corrective-cosmetics company author discussed why corrective cosmetics are needed, their history, how they are evaluated, the psychological impact of appearance, the attributes of an effective and acceptable concealer, and application methods [5].

A 2008 French multicentre study enrolled 90 patients receiving chemotherapy who had eyebrow loss, complexion changes or lip changes and had corrective makeup applied by trained aestheticians; 81.2 percent said it improved their overall quality of life and 76.8 percent reported enhanced self-esteem, and tolerance was rated satisfactory by most patients [6]. These studies concern camouflage makeup in medical settings rather than under-eye concealer in healthy people.

Forum posts include a guide on using concealer on dark circles without looking like makeup, and threads about how men can buy and hide concealer purchases. Posters describe borrowing a relative's product or concealing a purchase, which they attribute to social stigma around men's makeup.

In a thread about a concealer used on acne and scars after bonesmashing, the poster asks whether the product could worsen acne, illustrating that skin-concealing use extends beyond the eyes [9]. A 2021 questionnaire study of 539 Korean acne patients found that those who had failed earlier treatment were more likely than treatment-naive patients to say cosmetics worsened their acne (38.1 percent versus 26.3 percent), and noted that liquid foundation and concealer were frequently used; the authors recommended that dermatologists discuss cosmetic use with acne patients [10]. A formulation paper has also described an anti-acne concealer containing cinnamon oil tested against acne bacteria [11].

In looksmaxxing framings, concealer is usually placed with other low-barrier cosmetic changes, next to skincare, haircuts and grooming, and is discussed as something applied for photographs, dates or social situations.

No studies found on concealer as a treatment or on how detectable it is. Related studies examine dark-circle severity and corrective cosmetics generally: a 2021 study of 100 patients on correlates of periocular dark circles, a 1988 review of corrective cosmetics and a 2008 study of corrective make-up after chemotherapy [4][5][6].

lore.intro: Men on looksmaxxing forums discuss concealer as an accessible first cosmetic step, with discussion of discretion and shade matching.

claims.claim: Concealer can hide dark circles without looking like makeup.
Concealer is a hard-to-obtain item for men because of social stigma.
Colour-correcting tints cancel blue-purple circles better than a plain concealer.
Concealer can be used on acne and scars as well as under the eyes.
